assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines the magic-wavelength idea with laser-cooled neutral atoms to reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, far beyond the microwave definition of the second. It is a pure measurement advance of the kind that opens new physics: relativistic geodesy, tests of constancy of constants, dark-matter searches and a coming redefinition of the SI second. Strong fit to the view that progress is limited by what we can measure and how precisely.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme (2001-03) and demonstrated the first Sr lattice clock; Ye built the highest-performing systems and the comb-linked comparisons and the Sr clock accuracy records. Two names give a clean, defensible split. Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and others also contributed, and the Hall/Hänsch comb prize (2005) and Wineland's ion clocks (2012) already cover adjacent ground, so the credited pair is the natural core.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced in many national laboratories and in operation for over a decade, with intercomparisons and long-distance fibre links; the redefinition of the second is being prepared. Recognition is timely and not premature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes might lead some to see this as incremental, although the core idea and performance are distinct.
Whether Katori and Ye are enough, or whether other contributors such as Ludlow, Hinkley or Bloom should be counted, is a possible dispute that I cannot resolve from the supplied text.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms turned the wave nature of matter into a precision instrument: gravimeters, gradiometers, measurements of the fine-structure constant and G, and tests of the equivalence principle. A true measurement technique that has made new classes of experiments possible, and it is now moving into field and space-based sensing.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's Ramsey-Bordé atom interferometer and theory of light-pulse interferometry, Pritchard's grating-based interferometry and Kasevich's light-pulse gravimeters and gradiometers form a three-way split of roughly the right size. Chu's role is substantial but he is outside the credited list and already a laureate, and Chu/Kasevich overlap, so Kasevich's lineage carries part of it. Ordering of decisive credit among Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich, plus Chu, Mlynek, Keith and Kasevich-Chu 1991, is not fully clear.
assessment.maturity: Strong confirmation by many groups, with precision tests, commercial gravimeters and demonstrators of quantum-sensing applications. Interpretation is stable. A few headline applications, such as space-based tests, remain ahead, but the discovery is mature.
uncertainties: Attribution is crowded and historically contested, with several near-simultaneous 1991 demonstrations and credit connected to the 1997 cooling prize.
I have not independently verified specific record accuracies cited for particular experiments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed vacuum injected into interferometers beats the standard quantum limit and is now operating in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 to widen the detection volume. It marries a fundamental quantum-optics idea with a real instrument, showing the practical benefits of quantum states of light; a clear example of a measurement-sensitivity breakthrough.
assessment.attribution: Caves' 1981 proposal supplies the theoretical foundation, Kimble's group made the first squeezed states in 1985-86 together with Slusher's Bell Labs team, and Schnabel and the GEO600 group made it a working detector technology. Slusher, Yurke, Walls, Vahlbruch and others would be natural additional names, so the three-name configuration is plausible but leaves out real contributions.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing in gravitational-wave detectors has been operational since 2010 (GEO600) and in the LIGO O3/O4 runs, and is routine. Confirmation is strong, although the Nobel link to LIGO (2017) means the committee must consider overlap with that award.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should recognise squeezed light itself, the theory of quantum noise in interferometry, or the detector implementation is unclear.
The credited trio may omit key early experimenters such as Slusher or Wu.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Light-matter quantum interfaces and quantum memories are the enabling elements of quantum repeaters and networks. This includes entanglement of atomic ensembles, quantum-state transfer between light and atoms, and storage of single photons. It is close to my own area, so I know both its value and how hard the efficiency, bandwidth and storage-time requirements are in practice. The conceptual advance is clear; device-level impact is still emerging.
assessment.attribution: Polzik's continuous-variable ensemble experiments with teleportation and entanglement, Kimble's cavity-QED and DLCZ-type network vision and Lukin's EIT and ensemble theory plus experiments form a sensible configuration. The field is broad and includes rare-earth crystal memories (Afzelius, Tittel, Gisin and others) and DLCZ authors, so credit is spread more widely than the three names.
assessment.maturity: Many platforms (gases, crystals, cavities) demonstrate memories, but performance for a deployed quantum repeater is not yet routine. Mature as science, partly premature as a technology.
uncertainties: The discovery is compound, spanning several platforms and protocols, and different parts may need separate recognition.
Lukin appears in several candidate entries, so the committee may want to avoid assigning the same person across the shortlist.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single NV centres in diamond gave a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a nanoscale sensor for magnetic fields, temperature and electric fields, with uses in condensed matter, biology and NMR. This is a measurement tool that has expanded the range of observations, and applications keep growing.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko made the first single-centre optical detection and coherent control work; Lukin and collaborators (Hanson, Awschalom, Yacoby, Walsworth) extended it to sensing and long-lived memories. A three-person prize is possible but others have strong claims, for instance Awschalom, Hanson, and Budker/Walsworth in sensing.
assessment.maturity: Strongly replicated worldwide, with commercial instruments, though many applications are still developing. Timing is good, perhaps slightly early for the full application impact.
uncertainties: Attribution for sensing versus qubit control may require different groupings.
Whether the supplied three names capture the decisive credit given the size of the community.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and entanglement-based QKD established the idea that physical law, not computational assumption, can secure communication, and led to the field of quantum cryptography with working networks and satellite links. It is a conceptual contribution with demonstrated technology, and it is conceptually clear.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard created BB84 in 1984 and Ekert proposed the entanglement-based E91 in 1991; the three-way credit looks natural. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is a known and unresolved attribution point. Experimental demonstrations by many groups are not among the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Concepts have been demonstrated experimentally for decades, including satellite QKD, but practical security of implementations and deployment impact are still developing. The 2022 prize already recognised entanglement and Bell tests, which overlaps.
uncertainties: Ballot B016 is a near-duplicate entry; this ranking concerns the QKD idea only.
Overlap with the 2022 prize and the distance between theory and secure devices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type models with controllable parameters, as with the superfluid-Mott transition and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes, giving a measurement platform for many-body physics that could not be done otherwise. Conceptually and experimentally significant, with a strong link to quantum simulation.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott transition and microscopes. Credit for the single-site microscope is shared with Bakr, Greiner and Gross/Bloch, so allocation is uncertain; Jaksch, Hänsch, Esslinger and Kasevich also appear in the history.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced, with progress towards analogue quantum simulators. Mature, though the open questions about unique scientific discoveries made with simulators temper timing.
uncertainties: Boundary with the entries for Rydberg arrays and trapped-ion simulation.
Whether a quantum-simulation prize should wait for results that solve a standing problem.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical coherence tomography is a low-coherence interferometric technique that gave micrometre-resolution depth imaging of tissue and is now standard in ophthalmology. As a measurement method with wide use outside physics it fits my preference for new ways of observing, but the question is whether it is a physics discovery or an engineering-medical invention.
assessment.attribution: The 1991 Science paper by Huang, Swanson, Fujimoto and colleagues is credited, but the Fercher, Hitzenberger and Izatt contributions, and Fourier-domain OCT developments by Leitgeb, Choma and others, are not on the list, which makes the three-name configuration fragile.
assessment.maturity: Established clinically for decades with hundreds of millions of scans, so impact is clear and recognition if anything is late. Physics criteria for the prize might be debated.
uncertainties: Attribution across time-domain and Fourier-domain OCT is disputed.
Whether the committee would view it as sufficiently physics-centred.
